title: Ship to Play
summary: From a build on your laptop to an app Play accepts: the rules, the configuration, and the evidence that you can do it.

capstone.title: Ship it through a closed test
capstone.outcome: Run your own app through a closed test on OneDevs until 12 verified testers have used it across 14 days.

competencies.title: The closed-testing rule
competencies.outcome: Plan a closed test that meets Play's requirement for new personal developer accounts, and say what does and does not count.
model: A personal developer account created after 13 November 2023 cannot publish to production straight away. Play first asks for a closed test with at least 12 testers who have been opted in for at least the last 14 days continuously. Only then does the Dashboard let you apply for production access.

Opted in is the word that matters. An invitation is not a tester. A tester is on your list (an email list or a Google Group), opens the opt-in link, accepts, and installs from Play. Twelve invitations can be three testers.
Continuously means the last 14 days, not any 14 days. Someone who opts out stops counting, and someone who joins late has only the days since they joined. Recruit more than twelve: people leave.

Production access is an application, not a switch. Google asks how the test went and what you changed because of it, and it can say no. Testers who actually use the app and report problems give you something true to write.

code: Day 0   Create the closed track; upload a signed release AAB
Day 0   Add a Google Group of 16 people as the testers
Day 0   Share the opt-in link; testers accept and install
Day 1+  Testers use the app; you ship fixes to the same track
Day 14  12 or more have been opted in for 14 straight days
Day 14  Apply for production access from the Dashboard
notes: Sixteen, not twelve: anyone who opts out stops counting.
New builds during the test are fine. The rule is about testers, not builds.
Write down feedback and fixes as they happen; the application asks for them.

hints: The rule is about people, a number of days, and one word that describes their status.
Look for the answer built on being opted in, and staying opted in.

variants.prompt: What does Play require before a new personal account can apply for production access?
choices: At least 12 testers opted in to a closed test for at least the last 14 days continuously
At least 12 installs of the app at any time in the last month
20 five-star reviews from internal testers
14 testers for 12 days, followed by an open test
variants.why: Twelve testers opted in, for at least the last 14 days without a break. Installs, reviews and other tracks do not stand in for it.

variants.prompt: Which of these people counts toward Play's twelve?
choices: Someone in your Google Group who never opened the opt-in link
Someone who accepted the opt-in link and has stayed opted in
Someone you emailed an APK to
Someone who installed the app from production
variants.why: Only someone who accepted the opt-in and is still opted in counts. Being on the list, getting an APK, or using the production app does not.

hints: Count only the people who were opted in for every one of the last 14 days.
A tester who left, and a tester who joined late, are both short of 14 days.

variants.prompt: You start a closed test with 13 testers opted in. On day 9 two of them opt out. On day 14 you open the Dashboard. What do you see?
choices: You can apply: 13 were opted in at the start
You cannot apply yet: fewer than 12 have been opted in for the last 14 days
You can apply, because opting out does not remove anyone from the count
The test has been cancelled and the track deleted
variants.why: Eleven people have been opted in for the last 14 days. The two who left stopped counting the day they opted out.

variants.prompt: Your closed test started 20 days ago with 12 testers. Five days ago one of them opted out and someone new opted in. How many have been opted in for the last 14 days continuously?
choices: None: the count starts over
variants.why: The newcomer has five days and the one who left has none, so eleven have the full 14.

hints: Read each step against the rule: which track, who, how long.
One step points the build, or the testers, at the wrong place.

variants.prompt: Tap the step that means this plan can never meet the requirement.
code: Upload the release AAB to the internal testing track
Share the opt-in link the same day
Ship fixes to the same track as feedback arrives
Apply for production access on day 15
variants.why: The requirement is a closed test. Internal testing is a different track and does not count toward it.

variants.prompt: Tap the step that leaves you with no testers at all.
code: Create a closed testing track and upload the AAB
Add a Google Group with 15 members as testers
Send the group the link to the app's production listing
Ship fixes to the closed track as feedback arrives
Apply for production access after 14 days with 12 or more opted in
variants.why: There is no production listing yet, and a tester has to accept the opt-in link to count. The group needs the opt-in link, not a store link.

hints: Think about what makes the count drop, and what Google asks when you apply.
The good answer protects the count and gives you something true to say.

variants.prompt: You are about to start your test with exactly 12 people. What is the most useful change?
choices: Recruit a few more than 12, because anyone who opts out stops counting
Ask all 12 to uninstall after day 1 so the count is frozen
Upload a second build to start the clock
Move them to internal testing, which is faster
variants.why: Anyone who opts out stops counting, so exactly twelve leaves no margin. A few spare testers protect the 14 days.

variants.prompt: Your application for production access was turned down because the testing did not show enough engagement. What gives the next one the best chance?
choices: Run the test again with testers who use the app and report issues, and describe what you changed because of their feedback
Apply again the same day with the same answers
Add 100 people to the group without telling them about the app
Switch to an open test and skip the closed one
variants.why: Google wants to see a real test. Testers who use the app and report problems, and changes you made because of them, are what the application asks you to describe.

competencies.title: Exported components
competencies.outcome: Decide for every activity, service and receiver whether other apps may start it, and declare it so the build installs on Android 12 and later.
model: Every activity, service, receiver and provider in the manifest is a door into your app. android:exported says whether apps other than yours may open it.

From Android 12 (API 31), an activity, service or receiver with an intent filter must set android:exported explicitly. When the app targets 31 or higher and one does not, the manifest merger stops the build, and an APK like that would not install.
The launcher activity has to be exported, because the launcher is another app. Most other components should be exported="false": only your own code opens them.

An exported component with no permission can be started by any app, with any data in the intent. Treat what arrives in it as untrusted input. A signature permission limits the door to apps signed with your key.
Libraries bring components of their own. The merged manifest is the one that ships, and it is the one the Lab reads.

notes: MainActivity is exported because the launcher, another app, starts it.
SettingsActivity is opened only by your own code, so no other app needs the door.
An explicit false costs nothing and records the decision.

hints: Ask who opens the component: your own code, or another app.
Since Android 12, nothing with an intent filter is left to a default.

variants.prompt: Your app targets API 34. An activity has an intent filter and no android:exported. What happens?
choices: The build fails at manifest merge
It is exported by default
It is private by default
Only Play rejects it; local installs work
variants.why: Since Android 12 a component with an intent filter has to say whether it is exported. The merger refuses to guess, so the build stops.

variants.prompt: Which component has to be android:exported="true" in almost every app?
choices: The launcher activity
Every service
Every broadcast receiver
Any activity reached from a button in your app
variants.why: The launcher is another app, so the activity it starts has to be reachable from outside. Activities you open with your own buttons do not.

hints: Read the attributes: exported, and whether anything guards it.
A signature-level permission is granted only to apps signed with the same key.

variants.prompt: What can another app on the same phone do with this service?
choices: Start or bind to UploadService with any intent it likes
Nothing: services are never reachable from outside
Only read its logs
Only start it if it was installed from Play
variants.why: Exported with no permission is an open door: any app can start or bind to it, with any intent it likes.

variants.prompt: Which apps can start this service?
choices: Only apps signed with the same key as yours
Any app on the phone
No app, not even yours
Any app the user grants the permission to in a dialog
variants.why: The service is exported, but the permission guarding it has protectionLevel signature, which Android grants only to apps signed with your key.

hints: Look for a component that has an intent filter.
Of those, which one says nothing about being exported?

variants.prompt: This app targets API 34 and the build fails at manifest merge. Tap the line that starts the component causing it.
variants.why: ShareActivity has an intent filter and no android:exported. MainActivity says true, so it is fine.

variants.prompt: This app targets API 33 and the build fails at manifest merge. Tap the line that starts the component causing it.
variants.why: The receiver listens for BOOT_COMPLETED through an intent filter and does not say whether it is exported. AboutActivity has no filter and says false anyway.

hints: Who opens this component: your code, the system on another app's behalf, or another app?
A door that must be open still decides what it trusts.

variants.prompt: A library you added declares its own activity with an intent filter and no android:exported, and now your build fails. Your manifest is correct. What is the right fix?
choices: Update the library, or redeclare its activity in your manifest with android:exported set
Lower targetSdk to 30
Delete the library's manifest from the Gradle cache
Nothing: library manifests are ignored
variants.why: The merged manifest is what counts. Update the library to a version that declares it, or redeclare its activity in your manifest with android:exported set.

variants.prompt: Your app accepts text shared from other apps (ACTION_SEND). Which declaration is right?
choices: exported="true", and treat the incoming text as untrusted input
exported="false": the share sheet belongs to the system, so it still works
exported="true" with a signature permission
No intent filter; other apps can start it by class name
variants.why: The share sheet starts the activity on behalf of another app, so it must be exported. A signature permission would shut out every app not signed by you, and the text that arrives is input from a stranger.

competencies.title: Permissions and Play's restricted list
competencies.outcome: Ask only for the permissions a feature needs, when it needs them, and recognise the ones Play allows only with a declaration.
model: Install-time permissions such as INTERNET are granted when the app is installed. Runtime permissions such as CAMERA or ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION show a dialog: the person can say no, and change their mind later in Settings.

Ask in context, when the person taps the feature that needs it, not on first launch. A refusal is an answer the app has to handle, not an error. From Android 11, a person who denies the same permission twice is not asked again; the request returns denied.
Android 13 made notifications a runtime permission, POST_NOTIFICATIONS. An app that targets 33 or higher and never asks never notifies.

Some permissions are allowed on Play only for apps whose core purpose needs them, and only with a declaration in Play Console: SMS and Call Log, ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION, MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES and REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES among them. Ship one without qualifying and the update is rejected.

Often there is a way that needs no permission at all: the photo picker instead of reading media, a foreground service started while the app is open instead of background location. Libraries can add permissions too, so check the built APK, not only the manifest you wrote.

notes: The camera is asked for when the person taps Scan, so the dialog explains itself.
A refusal leads somewhere useful: typing the code by hand.
Nothing is asked at launch.

hints: Some permissions are granted at install; others need a dialog.
Since Android 13, notifications are among the ones that need a dialog.

variants.prompt: Which permission does Android grant at install, with no dialog?
choices: INTERNET
CAMERA
ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION
POST_NOTIFICATIONS
variants.why: INTERNET is an install-time permission. Camera, location and, from Android 13, notifications are runtime permissions.

variants.prompt: Your app targets API 34 and shows reminders. What must it do before its notifications appear on Android 13 and later?
choices: Request POST_NOTIFICATIONS at runtime
Nothing: notifications are always allowed
Declare FOREGROUND_SERVICE
Ask for SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM
variants.why: POST_NOTIFICATIONS is a runtime permission from Android 13. Without asking, the reminders never show.

hints: Android limits how often an app may ask, and merges library manifests into yours.
Two denials end the asking; a dependency can bring permissions of its own.

variants.prompt: The person has tapped Deny on your camera request twice. On Android 11 and later, what does launching the same request a third time do?
choices: Nothing visible: it returns denied without showing the dialog
It shows the dialog again
It opens Settings by itself
It throws a SecurityException
variants.why: Two denials count as 'don't ask again'. The request returns denied without a dialog; only Settings can grant it now.

variants.prompt: Your manifest lists only INTERNET, but the Lab's Permissions Inspector finds ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION in the built APK. What most likely happened?
choices: A library added it to the merged manifest
The Lab invented it
Android adds location to every app
Gradle adds it to apps built with Compose
variants.why: Library manifests are merged into yours. A dependency asked for location, and your app now does too.

hints: Match each permission to what the app says it does.
One of these is on Play's restricted list and the app's purpose does not need it.

variants.prompt: A barcode scanner that sends reminders. Tap the line Play will reject without a declaration this app cannot justify.
variants.why: QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES lets an app see every app installed, and Play allows it only for apps whose core purpose needs that. A scanner does not.

variants.prompt: A weather app shows the forecast for where you are when you open it. Tap the line that asks for more than that needs, and needs a Play declaration.
variants.why: Location while the app is open needs only coarse location. Background location is restricted on Play and needs a declaration and review.

hints: The best permission is the one you never need.
Is there a system component, or a moment when the app is visible, that does the job?

variants.prompt: A notes app lets people attach a photo they pick. Which approach needs no storage or media permission at all?
choices: The system photo picker
READ_MEDIA_IMAGES
MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE
READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE with requestLegacyExternalStorage
variants.why: The system photo picker hands the app only the photos the person chooses, and needs no permission.

variants.prompt: A running app records a route while the screen is off, after the runner pressed Start. Which shape avoids background location?
choices: A location foreground service started from the visible app, using while-in-use location
ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION requested on first launch
A WorkManager job every 15 minutes
MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE to write the route file
variants.why: A location foreground service started while the app is visible can keep using location granted 'while in use'. Background location is for apps that need it with nothing on screen.

competencies.title: targetSdk and Play's yearly floor
competencies.outcome: Set minSdk, compileSdk and targetSdk for what each one means, and keep targetSdk at or above Play's current floor.
model: minSdk is the oldest Android your app installs on. compileSdk is the API level you compile against: which classes and methods your code can name. targetSdk is a promise that you have tested against that version's behaviour, so Android applies its behaviour changes to you.

Raising targetSdk changes behaviour, not only a number: foreground services need a type when you target 34, and Android 15 draws apps edge to edge when you target 35. Read the version's behaviour changes and test before you raise it.
Every year Play raises its floor. New apps and updates must now target API {floor} or higher, and Play Console refuses an upload below it, however good the app is.

compileSdk should be at least targetSdk: you cannot promise to behave like a version you cannot compile against. To keep old phones and use new APIs, keep minSdk low and guard the new call with a check of Build.VERSION.SDK_INT.

code: minSdk = 26          // the oldest phone you support
targetSdk = {floor}  // the newest behaviour you tested
notes: minSdk and targetSdk answer different questions, so they are rarely the same number.
compileSdk is at least targetSdk.
The Lab compares targetSdk with Play's floor every time it reads an APK.

hints: One of the three is about the oldest phone, one about what your code can name, one about behaviour.
The oldest phone is minSdk's job; behaviour is targetSdk's.

variants.prompt: Which setting decides which behaviour changes Android applies to your app?
choices: targetSdk
minSdk
compileSdk
versionCode
variants.why: targetSdk tells Android which version's behaviour you have tested against, and Android applies that version's changes.

variants.prompt: Which setting decides the oldest Android version your app can be installed on?
choices: minSdk
targetSdk
compileSdk
A maximum version set in Play Console
variants.why: minSdk is the floor for installation. The other two are about compiling and behaviour.

hints: targetSdk decides two things: what Play accepts, and how Android treats the app.
Play checks updates as well as new apps, and Android applies the target's behaviour changes.

variants.prompt: Play's floor is API {floor}. You upload an update with targetSdk = {floor-1}. What happens?
choices: Play Console refuses the upload because of the target API requirement
It publishes, but only to phones on Android API {floor-1}
It publishes with a warning
It publishes: the floor applies to new apps only
variants.why: The floor applies to new apps and to updates. Play Console refuses the upload until targetSdk reaches it.

variants.prompt: You raise targetSdk from 34 to 35 and change nothing else. What do you need to check first?
choices: The behaviour changes Android 15 applies to apps that target it, such as edge-to-edge drawing
Nothing: targetSdk is only metadata
That minSdk is also 35
That versionCode starts again from 1
variants.why: Targeting 35 opts you into Android 15's behaviour changes, such as drawing edge to edge. The screens need testing before the update ships.

hints: Compare the three levels with each other and with Play's floor.
Which number is lower than one it has to be at least?

variants.prompt: This app must target Play's floor and use that version's APIs. Tap the line that is wrong.
variants.why: compileSdk 34 is below targetSdk {floor}. You cannot compile against the APIs of the version you promise to behave like.

variants.prompt: Play Console refuses this update. Tap the line responsible.
variants.why: targetSdk {floor-1} is below Play's floor of {floor}. compileSdk is already high enough.

hints: Each of the three numbers can move without the others.
The new API can be guarded at run time.

variants.prompt: Your app supports Android 8.0 and you want an API added in Android 13. What keeps both?
choices: Keep minSdk 26, compile against the latest, and guard the call with Build.VERSION.SDK_INT
Raise minSdk to 33
Lower targetSdk to 26
Lower compileSdk to 26
variants.why: minSdk stays where your users are, compileSdk lets you name the new API, and a version check calls it only where it exists.

variants.prompt: A library you depend on breaks when you raise targetSdk to Play's floor. What is the sound order of work?
choices: Update the library to a version that supports the new target, test the behaviour changes, then raise targetSdk
Keep targetSdk below the floor until the library is fixed
Raise minSdk instead
Remove the library's permissions
variants.why: Staying below the floor is not an option for updates. Update the library, test the behaviour changes, then raise targetSdk.

gate.task: Pick a release APK of your own app. The Lab reads its targetSdk and checks it against Play's floor of API {floor}.

competencies.title: App signing and your upload key
competencies.outcome: Sign release builds with your own upload key, explain what Play App Signing keeps, and keep the key out of the repository.
model: Android installs only signed apps, and an update has to be signed with the same key as the app it replaces. The signature is the app's identity.

With Play App Signing, which new apps published as App Bundles use, Google keeps the app signing key that signs what phones download. You sign what you upload with an upload key. If the upload key is lost, Play support can register a new one; the app signing key never leaves Google.
The Android SDK creates a debug key on every machine, under the name Android Debug. A build signed with it is a debug build whatever else it says, and Play Console refuses it.
Signature schemes: v1 is the old JAR signature, v2 (Android 7.0) signs the whole file, and v3 (Android 9) adds key rotation. Gradle applies the ones your minSdk needs.
The keystore and its passwords stay out of the repository: in a gitignored keystore.properties, or in your CI's secret store. A key that was ever committed has to be treated as public.

notes: The secrets come from a gitignored file, never from build.gradle.kts.
Only release uses the upload key; debug keeps the SDK's debug key.
OneDevs itself is built this way.

hints: There are two keys under Play App Signing. Which one stays with Google?
Which key could Play support replace for you?

variants.prompt: With Play App Signing, which key signs the APKs phones download from Play?
choices: Google's app signing key
Your upload key
The Android debug key
No key: Play removes signatures
variants.why: Google signs what it delivers with the app signing key it holds. Your upload key only proves an upload came from you.

variants.prompt: You have lost your upload key. What is true?
choices: Play support can register a new upload key; the app signing key is safe with Google
The app can never be updated again
You can sign with the debug key until it turns up
Uploading with any new key replaces the old one automatically
variants.why: The upload key can be reset through Play support, because Google holds the key that actually signs the app.

hints: A signature is identity: who built the app, and whether it is the same app.
The debug key proves nothing, and a different key means a different app.

variants.prompt: Your release AAB was signed with the debug config by mistake. What does Play Console do with the upload?
choices: Refuses it: it was signed in debug mode
Accepts it and signs it again with your upload key
Accepts it for closed testing only
Accepts it but hides it from search
variants.why: Play Console refuses anything signed in debug mode. The debug key is not yours alone and proves nothing.

variants.prompt: A phone has version 3 of your app, signed with key A. You install version 4, signed with key B. What happens?
choices: The install fails: an update must be signed with the same key
It installs and keeps the data
It installs as a second app
Android asks the person which key to trust
variants.why: An update must carry the same signing identity as the installed app, so Android refuses it.

hints: Read each line as Play Console would, then as someone reading the repository would.
One line hands over something that should come from elsewhere: a password, or the wrong key.

variants.prompt: This file is committed to git. Tap the line that leaks a secret.
variants.why: The keystore password is written into the build file, so everyone with the repository has it. Read it from a gitignored file or a CI secret, as the key password already is.

variants.prompt: Play Console refuses this release build. Tap the line responsible.
variants.why: The release build is signed with the debug configuration, so it carries the Android Debug certificate.

hints: Where do secrets live when no person should have to paste them?
The answer keeps the key out of git and out of inboxes.

variants.prompt: You move CI to a new provider. How should the release job get the upload key?
choices: From the CI's secret store, written to a file at build time and never committed
Committed to a private repository
Pasted into build.gradle.kts
Downloaded from Play Console
variants.why: The CI's secret store keeps the key encrypted and out of the repository; the job writes it to a file only while it builds.

variants.prompt: A teammate needs to make release builds on their own machine. What do you do?
choices: Give them access through a secret manager, so the key and passwords stay out of git and inboxes
Email them the .jks file and the passwords
Commit the .jks with the passwords removed
Let them generate their own upload key and upload with it
variants.why: Share access through a secret manager. A key sent by email or committed anywhere has to be treated as leaked, and a key they generate themselves is not the upload key Play knows.

gate.task: Pick a release APK of your own app. The Lab checks that it is signed with your own key, not the debug key, using a modern signature scheme.

competencies.title: Release builds: R8 and debuggable
competencies.outcome: Produce a release build that R8 has shrunk, that is not debuggable, and that still works where code is reached by reflection.
model: A release build must not be debuggable. A debuggable app lets anyone with adb attach a debugger and read its memory. Gradle's release type is not debuggable unless someone overrides it.
R8 shrinks (removes code nothing calls), optimises, and obfuscates (renames classes to a, b, c). isMinifyEnabled = true turns it on for release, and it is often the biggest size saving an app has.
R8 sees only the calls it can follow. Code reached by reflection, such as classes named in strings or models read by field name, needs a keep rule, or it is removed and crashes only in release.
Keep the mapping file R8 writes for every release, or stack traces arrive as a.b.c. An App Bundle carries it to Play; for an APK you upload it yourself.
Test the release build before it ships. The bug R8 introduces is invisible in debug, which is the build you test by hand.

code: // proguard-rules.pro: models read by field name over JSON
notes: Resource shrinking needs code shrinking on, which is why both are here.
The keep rule covers only what reflection reaches, not the whole app.
The Lab reads the R8 marker in the DEX to tell whether R8 actually ran.

hints: Think about what R8 does to code, and what a debugger can reach in a running app.
Shrinking and renaming is R8's job; reading memory is what a debugger allows.

variants.prompt: What does isMinifyEnabled = true turn on?
choices: R8: shrinking, optimisation and obfuscation of your code
Image compression only
Removal of unused languages
Debug symbols
variants.why: It runs R8 over the release build: shrinking, optimisation and obfuscation.

variants.prompt: Why must a release build not be debuggable?
choices: Anyone with adb can attach a debugger to it and read its memory
It runs slower, but only in the emulator
Play cannot read its icon
It cannot be signed
variants.why: A debuggable app accepts a debugger from anyone with adb, who can then read and change what it holds in memory.

hints: R8 renames and removes code; think about anything found by its name.
A renamed class can only be read back with the record of what it was renamed from.

variants.prompt: A class is filled from JSON by reflection, by field name. R8 is on and no keep rule covers it. What happens?
choices: Its fields are renamed or removed and parsing breaks, only in the release build
Nothing: R8 never touches data classes
The build fails
It works, but the APK is larger
variants.why: R8 renames or removes fields it does not see used, so parsing breaks, and only in release, which is why the debug build looked fine.

variants.prompt: A crash report from a release says: at a.b.c(Unknown Source). What do you need to read it?
choices: The mapping.txt R8 wrote for that exact build
The same crash from a debug build
The source code of the latest version
A new build with R8 turned off
variants.why: The mapping file R8 wrote for that exact build translates the short names back. Another build's mapping does not match.

hints: Read each line of the release block as if you were an attacker, then as if you were R8.
Which line turns off the thing the rules file is for, or turns on something release must never have?

variants.prompt: Tap the line that makes this release build unsafe to ship.
variants.why: isDebuggable = true makes the release build accept a debugger from anyone with adb.

variants.prompt: The rules file is there, yet the release APK is not shrunk. Tap the line responsible.
variants.why: R8 runs only when isMinifyEnabled is true. The rules file does nothing on its own.

hints: The fix should keep R8 working for the rest of the app.
Which build is the one your users actually get?

variants.prompt: After turning R8 on, the release build crashes on a screen that loads a class by name from a string. Debug is fine. What is the right fix?
choices: Add a keep rule for that class, then test the release build again
Turn R8 off for good
Make the release build debuggable
Rename the class to something shorter
variants.why: A keep rule for that class tells R8 it is used, and the rest of the app stays shrunk. Then test the release build itself.

variants.prompt: You want testers to see exactly what users will get. Which build do they install?
choices: The release build, signed and shrunk, from the closed track
The debug build from Android Studio
A release build with R8 turned off
Any build with the same versionName
variants.why: The signed, shrunk release build from the testing track is the one that behaves like production.

gate.task: Pick a release APK of your own app. The Lab checks that it is not debuggable or test-only, that its DEX was built for release, and that R8 ran.

competencies.title: App Bundles, ABIs and 16 KB pages
competencies.outcome: Ship native code that loads on every phone Play serves: 64-bit libraries alongside any 32-bit ones, aligned for 16 KB pages, delivered through an App Bundle.
model: New apps on Play are published as Android App Bundles (.aab). From the bundle Play builds APKs for each phone, so a phone downloads only its own screen density, CPU architecture (ABI) and, by default, languages.
Native code (.so files) is built once per ABI: arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86_64. An app that ships 32-bit native code has to ship the 64-bit version of it too.

Android 15 brought phones whose memory pages are 16 KB rather than 4 KB. A 64-bit library aligned only for 4 KB can fail to load on them. Play requires apps that target Android 15 or higher to support 16 KB pages, and NDK r28 and later align for it by default.
Native code usually arrives in a dependency, not in C++ you wrote. When the Lab finds an unaligned library, the fix is normally a newer version of whatever brought it.
An app written only in Kotlin or Java ships no native libraries, so there is nothing to align.

notes: Every 32-bit library has its 64-bit twin.
Every 64-bit library is aligned for 16 KB pages.
From a bundle, a phone downloads only the folder for its own ABI.

hints: A phone needs code for its own CPU, and Play builds what each phone gets from the bundle.
armeabi-v7a is 32-bit ARM; its 64-bit partner is arm64-v8a.

variants.prompt: What does Play deliver to a phone from your App Bundle?
choices: APKs holding only what that phone needs: its ABI, density and languages
The whole .aab file
A universal APK with every ABI
Only the code, with resources downloaded on first launch
variants.why: Play generates APKs from the bundle and serves each phone the parts for its own ABI, screen density and languages.

variants.prompt: Your app includes armeabi-v7a native libraries. What does Play require?
choices: The matching arm64-v8a libraries as well
Nothing else
x86 libraries
A separate listing for 32-bit phones
variants.why: 32-bit native code must come with its 64-bit version: arm64-v8a for ARM.

hints: Alignment is decided when the library is built, not at install.
Which apps have libraries at all?

variants.prompt: A 64-bit library aligned only for 4 KB pages is loaded on a phone with 16 KB pages. What can happen?
choices: It can fail to load, and the app crashes when it needs the library
It only loads more slowly
Android realigns it during install
Nothing: page size only matters for games
variants.why: The loader cannot map its segments, so the library can fail to load and the app crash when it needs it. Android does not realign it for you.

variants.prompt: Your app is written entirely in Kotlin and has no native dependencies. What do you need to do for 16 KB pages?
choices: Nothing: there are no native libraries to align
Rebuild with NDK r28
Set a page size in the manifest
Ship a 32-bit APK
variants.why: Alignment is about native libraries. With none in the APK, there is nothing to align.

hints: Pair each 32-bit library with its 64-bit twin, and read every 64-bit alignment.
One library is the odd one out.

variants.prompt: Play refuses this upload. Tap the library that causes it.
variants.why: libcrypto.so exists only for armeabi-v7a. 32-bit native code needs its 64-bit version alongside.

variants.prompt: This app targets Android 15. Tap the library that blocks the update.
variants.why: A 64-bit library aligned only for 4 KB does not meet the 16 KB requirement for apps targeting Android 15 or higher.

hints: Native code usually arrives with a dependency, and Play delivers per phone from a bundle.
Fix things at their source, and let Play send each phone only its own part.

variants.prompt: The Lab says libpdf.so is not aligned for 16 KB pages. You never wrote any C++. What do you do first?
choices: Find which dependency ships libpdf.so and update it to a version built for 16 KB pages
Delete the .so from the APK by hand
Lower targetSdk to 34 for good
Rename the file
variants.why: The library came from a dependency. A version of it built for 16 KB pages fixes it without touching the APK by hand.

variants.prompt: Your game ships native libraries for three ABIs and you want each phone's download as small as possible. What do you publish?
choices: An App Bundle, so each phone gets only its own ABI
A universal APK with every ABI
One app per ABI, each with its own listing
Only armeabi-v7a, to save space
variants.why: An App Bundle lets Play send each phone only the libraries for its own ABI.

gate.task: Pick a release APK of your own app. The Lab checks that any 32-bit native code has its 64-bit twin and that 64-bit libraries are aligned for 16 KB pages. An app with no native code passes.

competencies.title: Versions, tracks and staged rollouts
competencies.outcome: Number every upload correctly and move a release from testers to everyone in stages you can stop.
model: versionCode is the number Play and Android compare. Each upload needs a versionCode Play has never seen, and a phone updates only to a higher one. versionName is the text people read; nothing compares it.

Play's tracks run from narrow to wide: internal testing (up to 100 testers, available within minutes), closed testing (the track the twelve-tester rule is about), open testing (anyone can join), and production.
Promote a release rather than rebuilding it. The bundle your testers used is the one that should reach production.

A staged rollout releases to a percentage of users first. If crashes rise, halt it and Play stops offering the update to people who do not have it. Phones that already updated keep it, so you fix forward with a higher versionCode.
versionCode must stay at or below 2,100,000,000.

notes: One more than the highest code ever uploaded is the simplest rule that never fails.
versionName can say anything; versionCode cannot repeat.

hints: Play compares one number on every upload, and the twelve-tester rule names one track.
versionName is only text, and internal testing is not the closed track.

variants.prompt: Which value has to be new with every upload to Play?
choices: versionCode
versionName
targetSdk
minSdk
variants.why: Play compares versionCode and refuses one it has already seen. versionName is only text.

variants.prompt: Which track is the twelve-tester requirement about?
choices: Closed testing
Internal testing
Open testing
Production
variants.why: The requirement is a closed test. Internal and open testing do not count toward it.

hints: Ask what Play actually compares, and what it can still change on phones.
A versionCode is never reused, and a halt only stops new offers.

variants.prompt: Production has versionCode 41. You fix a typo and upload a new AAB with versionCode 41 and versionName 1.2.1. What happens?
choices: Play refuses it: versionCode 41 has already been used
It replaces 41
It publishes, because versionName changed
It publishes to testers only
variants.why: versionCode 41 has been used, so Play refuses the upload. Changing versionName changes nothing Play compares.

variants.prompt: You halt a staged rollout at 20%. What happens to people who already updated?
choices: They keep the update; you fix forward with a higher versionCode
Play rolls them back to the previous version
The app is removed from their phones
They are moved to the testing track
variants.why: Halting stops the update reaching anyone new. Those who have it keep it, so the fix goes out as a higher versionCode.

hints: Read the versionCode values only.
One number appears twice, or is outside what Play allows.

variants.prompt: Here is the upload history. Tap the upload Play refuses.
variants.why: versionCode 19 was already used by the second upload. Every upload needs a code Play has not seen.

variants.prompt: Play refuses an upload with this configuration. Tap the line responsible.
variants.why: versionCode is above Play's ceiling of 2,100,000,000.

hints: Which track is built for speed with a small trusted team?
The sound answer limits the damage first and fixes forward.

variants.prompt: You want new builds in front of a team of eight within minutes, several times a day. Which track?
choices: Internal testing
Production, with a 1% rollout
Open testing
Closed testing with a Google Group of twelve
variants.why: Internal testing exists for exactly this: up to 100 testers and builds available within minutes.

variants.prompt: Crashes jump after a 10% rollout. What is the sound sequence?
choices: Halt the rollout, fix, upload a higher versionCode, and stage it again
Go to 100% so the crash rate averages out
Delete the release from Play Console
Upload the same AAB again
variants.why: Halting stops the damage spreading; the fix goes out with a higher versionCode, staged again.

competencies.title: The store listing
competencies.outcome: Prepare a listing Play accepts that tells a stranger what the app does.
model: Text limits: the title is at most 30 characters, the short description at most 80, the full description at most 4,000. Play Console will not save a listing over them.

Graphics: the icon is a 512 by 512 PNG of up to 1 MB. The feature graphic is 1024 by 500, a JPEG or a PNG without transparency. Phone screenshots: at least two, each side between 320 and 3,840 pixels, and the long side no more than twice the short.
Play's metadata policy keeps the title, icon and developer name free of ranking claims and promotions: no 'best', '#1', 'free' or prices, no emoji used for decoration, no keyword lists.
The first line of the short description and the first screenshot carry most of the decision. Say what the app does and for whom, in words a stranger uses.
The Lab's store tools check your graphics and text against these rules before you upload.

code: Short description  Track spending in seconds, even offline.
notes: The title is the name, not a list of keywords.
The short description says what it does and the one thing that sets it apart.
1080 x 1920 is under the 2:1 limit and large enough to be featured.

hints: Recall the numbers: 30, 80 and 4,000 characters; 512 square, and 1024 by 500.
Only one of the graphics has to be opaque.

variants.prompt: How long can an app's title on Play be?
choices: 30 characters
50 characters
80 characters
There is no limit
variants.why: The title is limited to 30 characters. The short description has 80.

variants.prompt: Which feature graphic will Play accept?
choices: 1024 x 500, a JPEG or a PNG without transparency
512 x 512 PNG with transparency
1920 x 1080 in any format
1024 x 500 PNG with transparency
variants.why: The feature graphic is 1024 by 500, as a JPEG or a PNG without an alpha channel.

hints: Count the characters, then read the words against the metadata policy.
What does Play Console do with text over a limit?

variants.prompt: Your title is 'Best Free Budget App #1 - Save Money'. What will happen?
choices: It breaks the rules: it is too long, and 'best', '#1' and 'free' are not allowed in a title
It is fine, as long as the app is free
It is fine, as long as it fits in 30 characters
It is fine for a closed test
variants.why: It is over 30 characters, and 'best', 'free' and '#1' are the promotional words Play's metadata policy keeps out of titles.

variants.prompt: Your short description is 92 characters. What happens when you save the listing?
choices: Play Console will not save it until it is 80 characters or fewer
It is cut off with an ellipsis
It is accepted; the limit is a guideline
The extra text moves to the full description
variants.why: Play Console will not save text over its limit. Nothing is cut for you.

hints: Check every line against a number from the lesson.
Transparency, length, or proportions: one of them is wrong.

variants.prompt: Tap the part of this listing Play Console refuses.
code: Short description  Track spending in seconds, even offline.
Feature graphic    1024 x 500 PNG with transparency
variants.why: The feature graphic has transparency. Play wants a JPEG or a PNG without an alpha channel.

variants.prompt: Tap the part of this listing Play Console refuses.
code: Title              Pocket Ledger: Budget & Expense Tracker
Short description  Track spending in seconds, even offline.
variants.why: 'Pocket Ledger: Budget & Expense Tracker' is 39 characters, over the 30 a title may have.

hints: What does a stranger read first?
Words belong where they describe the app.

variants.prompt: Testers keep asking what your app is for. Where does the fix belong first?
choices: The first line of the short description and the first screenshot: what it does, for whom
A longer full description with more keywords
A new icon
A video at the end of the full description
variants.why: The short description's first line and the first screenshot are what people read before deciding.

variants.prompt: You want people searching for 'budget' to find you. What is within the rules?
choices: Use the word naturally where it describes the app, in the title or descriptions
Repeat 'budget' twenty times at the end of the full description
Put a competitor's app name in your title
Hide the word in tiny text inside a screenshot
variants.why: Using the word where it honestly describes the app is fine. Repetition, competitors' names and hidden text are what the policy forbids.

competencies.title: Data safety, privacy and account deletion
competencies.outcome: Declare what the app and its SDKs collect, publish a privacy policy, and give people a way to delete their account.
model: Every app on Play fills in the Data safety form: what data is collected or shared, why, whether it is encrypted in transit, and whether people can ask for it to be deleted. It covers your SDKs too. An ads or analytics SDK's collection is your app's collection.
Every app needs a privacy policy at a public URL, linked in Play Console. An app that handles personal data links it inside the app as well.

An app that lets people create an account has to let them delete it: from inside the app, and from a web page for people who no longer have it installed. Deleting means the account and its data, except what the law makes you keep, which you say.
The form has to match the build. Play reviews what the APK does and what its SDKs send; a form that says 'no data collected' over an analytics SDK is a policy violation.
If any ad shows, including through a mediation SDK, declare that the app contains ads.

code: Data type        Collected  Shared  Why                  Optional
Email address    Yes        No      Account management   No
Crash logs       Yes        No      App functionality    No
Device or ad ID  Yes        Yes     Advertising          Yes
notes: Sign-in brings the email address.
The crash reporting SDK brings crash logs.
The ads SDK brings the advertising ID, shared with the ad network.

hints: Responsibility follows the app: its SDKs and its accounts are yours.
Someone who uninstalled the app still needs a way to reach you.

variants.prompt: Who is responsible for declaring the data an analytics SDK in your app collects?
choices: You are: the SDK's collection is your app's collection
The SDK's vendor, in their own listing
Nobody: SDKs are exempt
Google, automatically
variants.why: You are. The SDK runs inside your app, so its collection is your app's collection.

variants.prompt: Your app has sign-up. What must it offer?
choices: Account deletion from inside the app and from a web page
Only an email address for deletion requests
Deletion after 12 months without sign-in
Nothing, if the privacy policy mentions data retention
variants.why: Account deletion from inside the app, and from a web page for people who have uninstalled it.

hints: Play compares what you declare with what the build does.
People without the app installed need a web page.

variants.prompt: Your Data safety form says 'No data collected', and the app includes an ads SDK that uses the advertising ID. What is likely in review?
choices: The update is rejected, or the app flagged, for an inaccurate Data safety form
Nothing: ads SDKs are exempt
Play fills in the form for you
Only people in Europe see a warning
variants.why: Play compares the form with what the build does. An inaccurate form gets the update rejected or the app flagged.

variants.prompt: Someone who uninstalled your app asks how to delete their account. What lets them do it?
choices: The deletion web page linked from your Play listing
Reinstalling and opening Settings, the only way
Emailing Google
Nothing: deletion needs the app
variants.why: The deletion web page linked from your Play listing exists for exactly this person.

hints: List what each SDK in the app collects, then compare it with the rows.
One row says 'not collected' about something an SDK in this app uses.

variants.prompt: Data safety draft for an app with Google sign-in, crash reporting and AdMob. Tap the row that is wrong.
variants.why: AdMob uses the advertising ID. The form has to say so.

variants.prompt: A release checklist for an app with accounts. Tap the line that falls short of Play's account deletion requirement.
code: Privacy policy URL added in Play Console
Data safety form matches the SDKs in this build
Account deletion: email support to request it
variants.why: An email to support is not deletion inside the app, and it is not a web page anyone can use. Play asks for both.

hints: A new SDK changes what the build does.
No accounts does not mean no data.

variants.prompt: You add a crash reporting SDK in an update. What else changes before you publish?
choices: The Data safety form and the privacy policy, to include what it collects
Nothing: crash data is anonymous
Only the versionName
The app's category
variants.why: The Data safety form and the privacy policy have to describe what the new SDK collects.

variants.prompt: Your app has no accounts and collects nothing itself, but it shows ads through an ads SDK. What do you still need?
choices: A privacy policy, an accurate Data safety form for the SDK's data, and the 'contains ads' declaration
Nothing at all
Only the 'contains ads' declaration
Account deletion
variants.why: A privacy policy, a Data safety form that declares the SDK's data, and the 'contains ads' declaration. Account deletion applies only to apps with accounts.
